title: Denmark and Gaines' Denmark, the Saddlebred's foundation
summary: Denmark, a Kentucky Thoroughbred foaled in 1839, sired Gaines' Denmark in 1851, and their line became the core of the American Saddlebred. The breed's registry was founded in Louisville in 1891, and in 1908 it named Denmark its sole foundation sire.
bodyMarkdown:
Denmark, a Kentucky Thoroughbred, is the horse that turned the Kentucky Saddler into a breed. Early Kentuckians needed a horse they could ride all day: across a farm, to court day, or over a rough road to the next county seat. Breeders crossed [Thoroughbreds with Narragansett Pacers and other easy-gaited stock](https://grokipedia.com/page/American_Saddlebred) and got a smooth, stylish riding horse they called the Kentucky Saddler. Kentucky's breeders [sold them across the young country](https://web.archive.org/web/20110921031759/www.saddlebred.com/Breed-History-1800).

## Denmark, 1839

Denmark was a [brown stallion foaled in Kentucky in 1839](https://grokipedia.com/page/denmark_%28horse%29), by the imported English horse Hedgeford out of a mare named Betsy Harrison. Sir Archy and Diomed, two of the great early sires of American racing, both appear in his pedigree. He was a racehorse by blood, but his lasting work was done in the breeding shed.

Bred to a part-bred mare known as the Stevenson mare, Denmark sired a black colt with two white hind socks. [Gaines' Denmark was foaled in 1851, bred by William V. Cromwell near Lexington](https://archive.org/details/registeramerica00assogoog/page/n40/mode/1up).

## Gaines' Denmark

The colt took his name from Edward P. Gaines, a breeder of saddle horses who lived near Georgetown and Lexington. In Scott County he was remembered as one of the most noted saddle stallions of early times, ["a great saddle horse" that "was never beaten in a fair ring."](https://npgallery.nps.gov/GetAsset/c25834fb-8b3c-4820-9c34-3079fda7608a) Before the Civil War he was shown and bred, and four of his sons, Washington Denmark, Diamond Denmark, Star Denmark and Sumpter Denmark, carried the line forward.

In 1857 a 16-year-old from Castleton Farm near Lexington, John B. Castleman, bought a three-year-old gelding named Lightfoot, a son of Gaines' Denmark out of a mare by Boston. Castleman trained him as a saddle show horse with the help of Isaac Byrd, an enslaved horseman held by the Castleman family. Lightfoot [sold for an unprecedented price](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaines%27_Denmark), and Castleman came to see Gaines' Denmark as a foundation sire for the saddle horse.

## Horses for the cavalry

When the Civil War came, offspring of Gaines' Denmark rode with the Confederate cavalry of [John Hunt Morgan](/people/#john-hunt-morgan). Morgan and Nathan Bedford Forrest [rode Kentucky Saddlers](https://web.archive.org/web/20110921031759/www.saddlebred.com/Breed-History-1800), and so did many officers on both sides, because a saddler could march all day and still carry a rider into a fight. Gaines' Denmark survived the war, though he did little as a sire afterward.

## A breed with a book

On April 7, 1891, breeders met in Louisville and [founded the National Saddle Horse Breeders' Association](https://grokipedia.com/page/American_Saddlebred), the first registry for an American horse breed. Castleman was among its founders and later its president. The association listed 17 foundation sires, and Denmark was one of them. More than 60 percent of the horses in the first three volumes of the studbook traced to Gaines' Denmark, and through him to Denmark.

In 1908 the directors [voted to make Denmark the sole foundation sire](https://grokipedia.com/page/denmark_%28horse%29). Harrison Chief joined him in 1991, the association's centennial year. For generations, people simply called Saddlebreds "Denmarks."

## Kentucky today

The breed's [World's Championship Horse Show](https://grokipedia.com/page/American_Saddlebred) is still held every August at the Kentucky State Fair in Louisville. The map pin is a town-level point in Lexington, near where he was bred; the exact farm is not known.
